n: Jacob looks up and sees Esau approaching with four hundred men. He divides the children among their mothers.
Jacob arranges his family in order, with Rachel and Joseph last—the safest position. The arrangement painfully shows who he loved most.

f.g: At the very back.

n: Jacob goes ahead of his family and bows to the ground seven times—a formal gesture of humble submission, as before a king.

f.w: bowed himself to the ground seven times
f.g: Ancient court documents describe vassals bowing seven times before a king.

n: Esau runs to Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck, and kisses him, and they both weep. Twenty years of anger melt away. Jesus’ parable of the prodigal son echoes this scene.

f.g: Threw his arms around him.

n: Esau asks who the women and children are. Jacob answers that they are gifts of God’s grace.

f.g: Given freely as a gift of grace.

n: The maidservants and their children approach and bow.

f.g: Bilhah and Zilpah.

n: Leah and her children bow next, and last Joseph and Rachel. Interestingly, Joseph is named before his mother—perhaps stepping forward to shield her.

f.w: after came Joseph near and Rachel
f.g: Joseph is mentioned first, perhaps hinting at his future prominence.

n: Esau asks about the herds he met. Jacob says they were meant to win his favor.

f.g: Herd or company.

n: Esau graciously replies that he has plenty and calls Jacob “my brother.” He does not need the gift.

f.g: Esau speaks as a brother, while Jacob keeps saying “my lord.”

n: Jacob insists, saying seeing Esau’s gracious face is like seeing the face of God. Having just met God at Peniel, Jacob now sees God’s grace in his brother’s forgiveness.

f.w: as though I had seen the face of God

n: Jacob urges Esau to accept his “blessing.” In a sense, Jacob gives back a blessing to the brother he had taken one from. Esau accepts.

f.g: Hebrew berakah—the same word for the blessing Jacob took (27:35-36).
Literally “I have everything.”

n: Esau offers to travel together, leading the way.

f.g: Esau offers to escort Jacob.

n: Jacob politely declines, explaining that the children and nursing animals cannot travel quickly. Driving them too hard would kill them—a caring shepherd’s concern.

f.g: Young and delicate.
Drive too hard.

n: Jacob suggests Esau go ahead while he follows slowly, promising to come to Seir.

f.g: Slowly; gently.
Jacob apparently never goes to Seir, perhaps wisely keeping his distance.

n: Esau offers some of his men as escort, but Jacob declines, asking only for continued goodwill.

f.g: “Why do that?”—there’s no need.

n: Esau returns that day to Seir. The brothers part in peace and later meet again to bury their father (35:29).
Jacob travels to Succoth, builds a house, and makes shelters for his animals. The name Succoth means “booths.”

f.g: Means “booths” or “shelters”; a town in the Jordan Valley (Judges 8:5).
Simple shelters, the same word as the later Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot).

n: Jacob arrives safely at the city of Shechem in Canaan, fulfilling his vow’s hope to return in peace. He camps outside the city.

f.g: Can mean “safely” or “in peace,” or be a place name.

n: Jacob buys a plot of land from Hamor’s sons for a hundred pieces of silver. Joseph’s bones would later be buried here, and Jesus talked with a Samaritan woman nearby at “Jacob’s well.”

f.w: bought a parcel of a field

f.g: Hebrew qesitah—a unit of value of uncertain weight.

n: Jacob builds an altar and names it “El-elohe-Israel”: “God, the God of Israel.” Using his new name, Jacob declares his personal faith.

f.g: “God, the God of Israel” or “Mighty is the God of Israel.”
